title: Insights into the Shape and Intensity of Plasmonic Fields in and around Individual Au/Ag@Au Nanorattles and their Conglomerations
content: Using noble metal nanomaterials as plasmonic catalysts continues to expand in efficacy for a number of economically important chemical reactions [1-2]. Of particular interest are plasmonic catalytic moieties made with the nanorattle morphology which have a holey outer shell and a free interior particle. Advantageously, this construct yields nanoconfinement of the reactants during the reaction within the shell, and most importantly, plasmon hybridization between the shell and the interior particle [3-4]. Although these materials have been used to great effect, a detailed mapping of the localized plasmon fields around the nanorattles as well as the relative impact of the two substituent groups, i.e. the shell and interior particle, remains poorly developed. Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) can be used to find the spatial intensity of the plasmonic fields around such materials by collecting the low energy range of the EELS spectrum from 0 – 10 eV [5]. We investigated Au/Ag@Au nanorattles which possess an Au particle core and void space enclosed by an Au/Ag composite holey shell [3]. Interestingly, the standard synthesis of these Au/Ag@Au nanorattles simultaneously generates three different sub-varieties of the nanorattle structure: relatively long, hexagonal, or round shell geometries (Figure 1). To map their plasmonic fields, we used a monochromated, aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (MAC-STEM; Hermes, Nion) to probe the low energy loss area of the EELS spectrum for each shell shape varietal. Additionally, we varied the Au/Ag ratio of the shell (0.2 or 0.4) to examine the impact of composition upon field intensity. By cross-comparing these individual particle types along with different aggregates which may form during catalysis such as dimers, small groups of four to six particles, and large masses (40+ particles), we gain a full picture of the plasmonic fields formed during catalytic processes, and the relative contributions each sub-type.
